q: In the shop, 6 customers placed 11 orders: 2 orders are guest orders (customer_id is NULL) and 2 customers never ordered. How many rows does customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id return?
explain: Measured: 11. The 9 orders that have a customer give 9 pairs, and the left join adds Dana and Farid with NULL order columns. The guest orders have no customer row to attach to, so only a FULL JOIN keeps them (13).

q: Ada has 4 paid orders with 500 of shipping each, and one of them has two items. What does sum(o.shipping_cents) return for Ada when the query joins orders and then order_items?
options: An error: shipping_cents is not grouped
explain: Measured: 2500. Joining the items repeats each order once per item, so the order with two items contributes its shipping twice: that is fan-out. Without the item join the sum is 2000; the fix is to aggregate items per order before joining.

q: Where do you put the condition for "customers with at least 2 paid orders"?
options: WHERE count(*) >= 2
In the ON clause of the join
HAVING count(*) >= 2
In ORDER BY, before LIMIT
explain: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates. The WHERE version fails with 42803: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE, because WHERE runs before the rows are grouped.

q: After customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id and GROUP BY c.id, what are count(*) and count(o.id) for Dana, who has no orders?
options: 0 and 0
1 and 1
0 and NULL
1 and 0
explain: Measured: 1 and 0. The left join keeps one row for Dana with NULL order columns; count(*) counts that row, and count(o.id) skips the NULL. That is why you count a column of the joined table after a left join.

q: Customers: 2 in Paris, 2 in Lyon, 2 with city NULL. How many rows does WHERE city <> 'Paris' return?
options: An error, because city is nullable
explain: Measured: 2, the Lyon customers. NULL <> 'Paris' is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. city IS DISTINCT FROM 'Paris' treats NULL as a value and returned 4.

q: Two customers never ordered, and two orders have a NULL customer_id. What does this query return?
code:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE c.id NOT IN (SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o);
options: The two customers who never ordered
An error: the subquery returns NULL
The two customers, plus one NULL row
No rows at all
explain: Measured: 0 rows. id NOT IN (…, NULL) expands to … AND id <> NULL, which is unknown, so the condition is never true. NOT EXISTS returned the expected two customers.

q: On PostgreSQL 18, what happens to a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE that the main query references once?
options: It is inlined into the main query, so outer filters can reach the table
It is always computed first and stored, as an optimisation fence
It is computed once per row of the main query
It is cached between executions of the same query
explain: Since PostgreSQL 12 such a CTE is folded into the main query; EXPLAIN showed an index scan on orders with the outer id = 101 filter. The fence behaviour is what you get when you add MATERIALIZED, or by default when the CTE is referenced twice.

q: "Latest paid order per customer" uses a LATERAL subquery with LIMIT 1. What is the difference between CROSS JOIN LATERAL (…) and LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) ON true?
options: None: LATERAL always keeps every outer row, with or without LEFT
The LEFT JOIN form keeps customers for whom the subquery returns no row, with NULL columns
The CROSS JOIN form runs the subquery once instead of once per customer
Only the LEFT JOIN form may refer to columns of customers inside the subquery
explain: Measured: CROSS JOIN LATERAL returned Ada, Brendan and Chen; LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true also kept Dana, Eve and Farid with NULL. Both forms run the subquery per outer row and both may refer to outer columns: that is what LATERAL means.

q: Paid order totals, highest first: 20000, 6000, 5000, 4000, 3000, 3000, 3000, 3000, 500. What do rank() and dense_rank() give the 500 order?
options: 6 and 6
9 and 9
9 and 6
6 and 9
explain: Measured: rank 9, because the four tied orders share rank 5 and the next rank skips to 9; dense_rank 6, because it leaves no gaps. row_number also gives 9 but numbers the tied rows 5 to 8 in an arbitrary order.

q: What is the default frame of sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)?
options: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes the peers of the current row
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, one physical row at a time
The whole partition, as without ORDER BY
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
explain: The PostgreSQL docs state the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, that is up to the current row's last peer. Measured: ordered by month, the three January orders all showed 8500; with an explicit ROWS frame they showed 5000, 8000, 8500.

q: MS-01 already exists. What does INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price_cents) VALUES ('MS-01', 'Mouse', 3000) ON CONFLICT (sku) DO NOTHING RETURNING id return?
options: The id of the existing mouse
A unique violation error
A row with a NULL id
No row at all
explain: Measured: 0 rows. RETURNING only reports rows the statement inserted or updated, and DO NOTHING touched none. Code that needs the existing id must read it with a separate SELECT, or use DO UPDATE.

q: In INSERT … ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET price_cents = EXCLUDED.price_cents, what does EXCLUDED hold?
options: The row already stored in products, before the update
The values the statement tried to insert for the conflicting row
The rows that the conflict check removed from the result
The previous price, as RETURNING old reports it
explain: EXCLUDED is the row proposed for insertion, so the SET copies the feed's price onto the existing row: measured, the mouse went from 3000 to 3100 and kept its id. The existing row is read through the table name, products.price_cents, as in the lesson's WHERE … IS DISTINCT FROM.

q: A back-office list must show every customer with their number of paid orders, including 0. It shows only Ada, Brendan and Chen. Which fix would you ship?
code:
SELECT c.name, count(o.id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id;
options: Move o.status = 'paid' into the ON clause
Replace LEFT JOIN with FULL JOIN
Replace count(o.id) with count(*)
Change the filter to WHERE o.status = 'paid' OR o.status IS NULL
explain: Measured: with the condition in ON, all 6 customers came back, Dana, Eve and Farid with 0. The OR o.status IS NULL patch is tempting but returned 5 rows: Eve disappeared, because her joined row carries a cancelled status, not NULL.

q: A revenue report joins customers, orders and order_items, then sums o.shipping_cents and the item amounts per customer. The shipping total is too high for customers whose orders have several items. Which change is correct?
options: Use sum(DISTINCT o.shipping_cents)
Aggregate order_items to one row per order in a CTE, then join that to orders
Use count(DISTINCT o.id) next to the sum
Add i.product_id to the GROUP BY
explain: Aggregating the child per parent first means each order meets the customer as one row; measured, Ada's shipping went from 2500 back to 2000. sum(DISTINCT …) removes equal amounts, not duplicate orders: it gave 500 for Ada's four orders at 500.

q: Eve has one cancelled order and no paid one. What does the API receive in shipping_paid for her?
code:
SELECT c.name,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')           AS paid,
       sum(o.shipping_cents) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid') AS shipping_paid
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;
options: 0, like the paid count
500, the shipping of her cancelled order
NULL
An error: FILTER cannot be used with sum
explain: Measured: paid 0 and shipping_paid NULL. count over zero rows is 0, but sum over zero rows is NULL, and FILTER left no row for the sum. Wrap it in coalesce(…, 0) if the API contract says number.

q: In review, a colleague says this query will fail because c.name and c.city are not in the GROUP BY. What do you answer?
code:
SELECT c.name, c.city, count(*) AS orders
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;
options: They are right: every selected column must be listed in GROUP BY
It runs, but picks an arbitrary name per group
It runs only if name and city are NOT NULL
It runs: c.id is the primary key, so the other columns of customers depend on it
explain: Measured: the query runs and returned 4 rows. Grouping by a table's primary key lets you select that table's other columns, because each group has exactly one value for them. Nothing is arbitrary: each group is one customer, so it has exactly one name and one city.

q: A profile endpoint skips no-op writes with this statement. A user whose city is NULL sets it to Lyon. What happens?
options: Nothing is updated: NULL <> 'Lyon' is unknown, so the row is filtered out
The row is updated, because NULL differs from any value
The statement fails because city is nullable
The row is updated, but a RETURNING city clause would show NULL for it
explain: Measured: 0 rows updated for Chen. With city IS DISTINCT FROM $1 the update went through, and RETURNING old.city, new.city showed NULL then Lyon. A comparison with NULL is never true, whatever the intuition says.

q: "Products never sold": both NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items) and NOT EXISTS (…) return the dock today, and order_items.product_id is NOT NULL. Why would you still ship NOT EXISTS?
options: NOT IN with a subquery is deprecated since PostgreSQL 18 and logs a warning
It stays correct if the subquery ever yields a NULL, and the planner runs it as an anti-join
NOT IN cannot use a subquery on another table
NOT EXISTS returns the rows in primary key order, which keeps API responses stable
explain: The NOT IN result depends on the subquery never containing NULL, which a later change can break silently. On this data EXPLAIN showed a Hash Right Anti Join for NOT EXISTS and a filter over a hashed subplan for NOT IN. NOT IN is not deprecated; it is just fragile.

q: This endpoint worked in development, where each customer had one order. What happens in production?
options: It returns one row per order, like a join
It returns the first order of each customer
It fails with 21000: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
It returns NULL for customers with several orders
explain: Measured: the query fails as soon as one customer has two orders. A scalar subquery must return at most one row; it never multiplies rows like a join, and without ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 there is no "first". Use a LATERAL subquery or an aggregate to say which order you want.

q: A query joins a CTE paid to itself (FROM paid a JOIN paid b …). With no keyword after AS, what does PostgreSQL 18 do?
options: It inlines both references, as for any non-recursive CTE
It rejects the query: a CTE can be referenced only once
It computes the CTE twice, once per reference
It computes the CTE once, stores it, and scans the stored result twice
explain: Measured with EXPLAIN: one CTE paid node with two CTE Scans. The docs say folding happens by default only when the CTE is referenced once; NOT MATERIALIZED forced inlining, and the plan then showed two index scans on orders.

q: What is wrong with this query?
code:
SELECT c.name, x.id
FROM customers c,
     (SELECT o.id FROM orders o
      WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      ORDER BY o.placed_on DESC LIMIT 1) AS x;
options: A subquery in FROM cannot see c without LATERAL: it fails with 42P01
It runs, but returns only the latest order overall
A subquery in FROM cannot use LIMIT
It runs, but returns every customer, Dana included
explain: Measured: 42P01: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "c". Adding LATERAL before the subquery makes it run once per customer. Even fixed, the comma form behaves like CROSS JOIN LATERAL and drops customers without orders, so Dana would not appear.

q: A leaderboard endpoint pages orders with row_number() OVER (ORDER BY total_cents DESC). Its tests fail now and then: the same order appears on two pages. What is the fix?
options: Replace row_number with rank
Add a unique tiebreaker: ORDER BY total_cents DESC, id
Add PARTITION BY total_cents
Wrap the query in a CTE marked MATERIALIZED
explain: Tied totals have no defined order: measured, the four orders at 3000 came out as 104, 103, 102, 110, an order nobody chose. A unique last column makes the numbering deterministic. rank would give the tied rows the same number, which breaks paging differently.

q: January has three paid orders: 101 (5000), 103 (3000) and 108 (500), one row each in the CTE january_order_totals. What does this query show for order 101?
code:
SELECT id, total_cents,
       sum(total_cents) OVER (ORDER BY date_trunc('month', placed_on)) AS running
FROM january_order_totals
ORDER BY placed_on, id;
explain: Measured: 8500 on all three rows. The default frame is RANGE … CURRENT ROW, and the three orders share the same month, so they are peers and each sees the whole month. With ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW the column read 5000, 8000, 8500.

q: A monthly revenue report computes revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) from GROUP BY month. March had no paid order, and April shows a change of -13000. What is wrong?
options: lag needs PARTITION BY month, otherwise it reads across every month of the report
The default RANGE frame includes peers, so April is summed together with February
lag reads the previous row, February, because March has no row; generate the months with generate_series and left join the revenue
date_trunc returns a timestamp, so the months are sorted as text and not in calendar order
explain: Measured: the grouped result had rows for January, February and April only, so April was compared with February (13000 - 26000). After building the four months with generate_series and coalesce(revenue, 0), March showed -26000 and April +13000. Frames do not affect lag.

q: For the CRM screen, a colleague writes this query to get each customer's latest paid order. What happens?
code:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, placed_on
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
ORDER BY placed_on DESC;
options: It returns the latest paid order of the whole shop, once
It returns one arbitrary paid order per customer
It returns every paid order, newest first
It fails with 42P10: the DISTINCT ON columns must start the ORDER BY
explain: Measured: 42P10: SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions. DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group in the sort order, so the sort must begin with the group: ORDER BY customer_id, placed_on DESC, id DESC returned 102, 107 and 108. PostgreSQL rejects the query before reading a row, so it returns neither an arbitrary order nor a global latest.

q: "The 2 latest orders of each customer" on 1,000 customers and 100,000 orders, with an index on orders (customer_id, placed_on DESC, id DESC). Which pattern reads the fewest rows?
options: CROSS JOIN LATERAL with ORDER BY … LIMIT 2
row_number() in a CTE, filtered on <= 2
DISTINCT ON (customer_id) run twice
ORDER BY placed_on DESC LIMIT 2000
explain: Measured on PGlite: the LATERAL plan read 2,000 index rows (2 per customer, 1,000 index searches), while row_number read all 100,000 even with its Run Condition. A global LIMIT 2000 does not give 2 per customer, and DISTINCT ON returns one row per group.

q: Ada's paid orders total 5000, 3000, 3000 and 3000. Product asks for "her top 3 orders" and you use rank() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total_cents DESC) <= 3. How many rows does Ada get?
explain: Measured: 4. The three orders at 3000 all get rank 2, which is within 3. row_number would return exactly 3 and cut a tie arbitrarily unless you add a tiebreaker. Ask product which one they mean: that question is the point of the exercise.

q: A catalogue import upserts 500 rows in one INSERT … ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE. One night it fails with 21000: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: Another transaction updated the same rows; retry the statement
The table has no unique index on sku; add one
The feed contains the same SKU twice; deduplicate the batch before the upsert
The batch is too large; split it into chunks of 100
explain: Measured: two rows with the same SKU in one statement raise exactly this error, and its hint says to ensure no duplicate constrained values in the proposed rows. A missing unique index gives a different error (42P10: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification), and chunking only helps if the duplicates land in different chunks, which is luck.

q: A payment webhook must insert a payment by its provider id, or update it when it already exists, and the provider may deliver the same event twice at the same time. Which statement would you ship?
options: MERGE, because it is the SQL standard
A SELECT then an INSERT or UPDATE from Node
UPDATE, then INSERT if no row was updated
INSERT … ON CONFLICT (provider_id) DO UPDATE
explain: The PostgreSQL MERGE docs point to INSERT … ON CONFLICT because it can still run its UPDATE when a concurrent transaction inserts the same key; the Transaction Isolation chapter states that MERGE raises a uniqueness violation in that case. The read-then-write versions race in the same way (M09).

q: A churn report shows the days since each customer's previous paid order. Brendan's first order (2026-02-14) shows -56. What is the bug?
code:
SELECT customer_id, id, placed_on,
       placed_on - lag(placed_on) OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, placed_on, id) AS days_since_previous
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY customer_id, placed_on, id;
options: The window has no PARTITION BY customer_id, so Brendan's first order is compared with Ada's last one
The default RANGE frame includes peers, so lag reads an order placed on the same day
lag needs an explicit ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW frame
The rows are sorted by customer_id first, so lag reads the next order instead of the previous one
explain: Measured: without a partition the window is the whole result, so Brendan's first order was compared with Ada's last one (2026-04-11): -56 days. With PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_on, id, each customer's first order got NULL and Brendan's second got 47. Frames do not affect lag: it always reads the previous row of its partition.
